extracted.intended_audience: scientists and researchers preparing grant proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for scientists preparing funding applications, focused on making proposals clear, well-structured, persuasive, and appropriately detailed for reviewers. Emphasises readability, narrative/problem framing, layout, methodological detail, and concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: The level of difficulty doesn’t match the reviewers’ background and time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the proposal is understandable to reviewers who may not share deep, topic-specific background and who have limited time to assess it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear structure (storytelling structure recommended) and good flow so sentences/paragraphs link and information builds gradually. Avoid assuming too much pre-existing knowledge and don’t expect reviewers to spend lots of time deciphering your text. Use consistent terminology (avoid different synonyms for the same concept) and introduce topic-specific jargon before using it. Prefer verbs over noun-heavy constructions and avoid complicated sentence constructions that sound ‘fancy but incomprehensible.’

rubrics_metrics.name: You haven’t identified a problem your research will solve
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the proposal as a narrative that makes clear the problem (tension) your research addresses so reviewers are interested and see the importance of the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a narrative by identifying a clear problem/gap early and angle background information to show how your project will solve it. Use the element of tension to create curiosity and justify the proposed work—this is not storytelling fiction but a structured presentation of problem → gap → proposed solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: The page layout is overwhelming
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation and formatting matter: a dense, wall-of-text layout reduces reviewer motivation and comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic differentiation (fonts, sizes, bold/italic) to separate sections, subsections, figure captions and main text. Highlight important sentences judiciously (don’t overdo it). Use white space effectively by adjusting spacing and indents; avoid very long paragraphs (recommended paragraph length 100–200 words). Do not have single paragraphs span half a page; break text into readable chunks.

rubrics_metrics.name: You don’t provide enough detail about HOW you are planning to do your research
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers need concrete evidence that the project is well thought-through, feasible, and that the team can execute it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specifics such as a timeline (e.g., Gantt chart), risk management plan, budget, and descriptions of personnel roles and collaborations—even if not explicitly requested. Be specific about who you will collaborate with, why they are suitable, and why the collaboration is needed. Balance specificity with relevance: include enough detail to show feasibility but omit operational minutiae only needed by those actually doing the experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: You provide redundant information
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repetition and unnecessary length while keeping necessary context; redundancy wastes limited space and reviewer attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constrained by page/word limits, do not sacrifice white space to cram more text. Edit carefully to remove repeated ideas and duplicate wording—read every sentence (or word) to find repetitions. However, do not delete information that helps reviewers understand the idea and context (e.g., brief reminders of the gap being addressed can be appropriate). Aim for concise description of the proposed research.
